It’s not like Mydei never wanted this life for himself.

If anything, everything he had done thus far had led up to this. From all the lessons he took up learning the guitar (both its acoustic and electric variants), to all the covers he’d been secretly recording and uploading, to finally getting his own contract and manager with a record label–they all molded him to undertake the weight of this moment. After years of pining for a shot in the limelight, he finally had his own opportunity served to him on a silver plate.

Still, no matter how glorious and exciting all these were, the fact that he was going to be the opening act for an incredibly popular rock band made him nervous.

“Do you have everything you need with you already?”

Mydei glanced at his phone now, his attention shifting from his thoughts and back towards the present. Taking up the entirety of its screen was his mother, Gorgo, who had her own gaze averted from Mydei. She looked like she was preoccupied with the drive home, but Mydei knew her attention was divided between the road and him.

Not wanting to make her any more distracted than she already was, Mydei answered her promptly. “I do,” he reassured her. “All the band equipment arrived earlier, including mine.”

He looked around at his large but otherwise empty hotel room. He had just checked in earlier this afternoon, and this suite was to be the place of his residence for a few more days until the tour officially began. And though he had taken his luggage and both of his guitars with him—leaving his speakers, amplifiers, and other equipment under the care of the logistics team—there was still more than enough room for one.

It was a luxury Mydei had only once dreamed of.

However, to the band he was traveling with, this was mere reality. To the Flame-Chasers, this was just another day in their superstar life.

He looked back at his mother. “Don’t worry about me,” he added, soothing her yet again. “I’m fine.”

She snorted. Passing streetlights bathed her in alternating shows of light and shadow. “It is futile to tell a mother not to worry about her own child, no matter how grown that child may be,” she chastised. She glanced at him briefly. “Especially if her son in question is about to embark on his first tour across the country.”

Mydei rested his chin in his hand. “You have full access to every one of those shows should you wish to come see me in one.”

“And I will,” she promised. Though her eyes were on the dashboard, the camera caught the way her expression softened. “Though I regret not being there with you at your first one. This was all you dreamt of when you were younger.”

“Mom,” Mydei said, smiling fondly, “I’m fine. I’ll make sure to send you all the photos and videos I can.”

“You better.”

Before either of them could make another remark, their conversation was promptly interrupted by the ringing of the doorbell. Mydei schooled his features back into neutrality as he rose to his feet, taking his phone with him as he padded to the door.

“Expecting a visitor at this time?” If he didn’t know any better, Mydei would have thought his mother sounded almost teasing.

“No,” he said. He glared at her, though she couldn’t see him. “Why do you make it sound like that?”

“It was just a question, my love,” she replied, attempting to dismiss Mydei’s suspicions. “No need to get all defensive.”

Mydei rolled his eyes. He peered into the peephole of his door, ascertaining who had come to check on him. Then he turned the lock, pressed the handle, and swung the door open for the man standing on the other side of the door.

Mydei had already seen him through the peephole. But it still surprised him to find the lead singer of the Flame-Chasers truly waiting for him on the other side. He was whistling a song from his own band as he waited, though he quickly fell silent upon finding himself face-to-face with Mydei.

Away from the public eye, Phainon was dressed in a simple garment of a plain hoodie and a pair of loose sweatpants. When he beheld Mydei—who was dressed similarly, just in dark colors as opposed to Phainon—he grinned.

“Hello,” Phainon greeted. He looked like he was about to say something more when his eyes caught sight of Mydei’s phone in his hand. Then his expression shifted, and his smile turned a little more polite than it just was. “Did I catch you at a bad time?”

“It’s fine.” Mydei turned the phone, revealing the image of Gorgo on its screen. “I was just talking to my mother.”

Phainon ducked, presumably within view of the camera, and waved. “Hi, ma’am!”

“Hello, Phainon,” Mydei heard her greet in return. “It’s a little late, isn’t it?”

Mydei immediately averted his phone from Phainon. “Yes,” he interrupted, answering on his behalf. “Which is why it’s best for us to get some rest.”

Phainon, either oblivious to Gorgo’s subtle teasing or deliberately ignorant of it, nodded. “I was just checking up on Mydei to see how he was settling in.”

“How chivalrous of you,” Gorgo crooned. “Thank you for taking care of my son.”

Mydei rubbed the spot between his brows. “I’ll call you again tomorrow,” he said, dismissing her as gently as possible. “Drive safely, and text me when you get home.”

“Alright.” On the video, Gorgo pressed two fingers to her lips before tapping them against her own camera. “Love you.”

Mydei mimicked her gesture, kissing two of his fingers before placing them over his phone. “Love you too.”

As soon as both of them hung up, Mydei pocketed his phone in the pocket of his pants. Then he crossed his arms over his chest, all his softness melting away, and looked at Phainon. “What are you doing here?”

Phainon remained standing just outside of the doorway. He made no move to invite himself inside, and Mydei made no move to invite him either.

“Like I said,” he reiterated, his politeness giving way to his usual teasing self, “I’m here to make sure you’re settling in alright.”

Mydei angled his body and gestured at the neatness of his room. “Everything’s in order,” he said concisely.

Phainon pouted. “No room tour?”

Mydei looked at him with incredulity. “We have the same kind of suite.”

Phainon sighed, looking forlorn as he leaned against the doorway. “You’re so much nicer when your mom is around.”

Mydei heaved his own sigh, though he only looked exasperated by it all. “If there’s nothing else, I would like to get some rest. I’m fine, but I’m a little tired.”

“Really?” Phainon took a half step closer. “I still remember the days leading up to my first tour. I could hardly eat or sleep from the anxiety of it all.”

“So? Are you still anxious now?”

“Only a little. But I’m here to make sure you don’t lose yourself in that same overwhelming feeling.”

“Are you really?” Mydei asked. “Or are you just here to ensure I don’t fuck up the opening act?”

Phainon laughed. “Hey now! What do you take me for?” He paused in consideration before finally adding, “Can’t it be both?”

Mydei shot him a look. “There it is. Your faux concern.”

“It’s not a pretense! I really am concerned!” Phainon shook his head with a sigh. “Honestly, Mydei. You doubt my intentions a little too much.”

“For good reason,” Mydei said under his breath, though his words seemed to be lost on Phainon as he continued to talk.

“You know,” he began, crossing his arms over his chest and leaning against the wall, “you’re a lot more attractive if you’re only singing and playing the guitar.”

Mydei frowned at the backhanded compliment. Then, in the hopes of turning this situation on him and catching him tongue tied instead, he raised a brow. “You find me attractive?”

Unfazed, Phainon shrugged. “So what if I do? It doesn’t mean anything.”

He almost convinced both of them that it was nothing. But Phainon’s expression darkened, just a little bit, and he glanced at Mydei once more. “Unless, of course, you want it to.”

Mydei narrowed his eyes. “What does that mean this time?”

“Whatever you want it to mean.”

They stared at one another, their shared gaze an impasse. Then Phainon smiled cryptically, dismissively, and he pushed himself off the wall.

“Anyways,” he said with a wave of his hand. “It’s getting late, and I want to get as much sleep as I can before the tour begins in a few days.”

He turned on his heel. “Good night, Mydei. If you need anything, I’m just a room away.” He looked over his shoulder, blue eyes hooking in Mydei’s golden ones. “And, if you need anything else, know that our previous arrangement still stands.”

He turned away and Mydei watched him go, his eyes tracing every inch of his back: from the top of his head, to his waist, to the heels of his feet. Though the clothing he wore was a size too big on him, Mydei could almost imagine the tautness of his muscles, the shape of his waist, and the curves of his body beneath the layers.

He found himself clenching his jaw, considering.

Phainon may be telling the whole truth, but Mydei was definitely a little dishonest with himself. For all his show of confidence, he was a little nervous for the tour.

So, with his best attempts to swallow his pride, Mydei cleared his throat. “Phainon.”

Phainon paused. He glanced at Mydei, eyes wide with innocence. “Hmm?”

Mydei’s fingers tightened against his arms. Was Phainon going to make him spell it out? “I may be a little high strung,” he said in a quiet voice.

Phainon smiled. He turned fully and made his way back to Mydei. “Now what does that mean this time?”

Mydei scowled as Phainon entered his personal space. He hated it when his own words were thrown back at him, and he hated it when someone was far too close to him.

And yet.

Phainon continued taking a step forward until he had one leg pressed between Mydei’s. His thigh rubbed against his groin as he snaked an arm around Mydei’s waist.

“Are you, perhaps, looking for a way to blow off some steam?” he asked, pulling him closer. His eyes dropped down to Mydei’s lips once, but he made no move to further close the distance between them.

Mydei stiffened. Despite himself, he found himself leaning in closer and closer. “Don’t make me regret this.”

Phainon only grinned in response. Then he was pushing against Mydei, leading them both back inside the privacy of the suite, before closing the door behind him.

Mydei could deny this as much as he wanted to. But as they fell in a tangle of limbs and lust, articles of clothing slowly falling apart between them, he knew it was futile to do so.

After all, this wasn’t their first time. Nor was it their second, nor was it their third.

From the moment Mydei met Phainon, he was ensnared with two arrangements. Both bore different loads of responsibility, but both were of his own volition.

The first was his contract with Phainon and the Flame-Chasers, a promise that Mydei would be their opening act for their music tour this year.

The second, Mydei thought, as he and Phainon finally stumbled into his bed, was this.

A Few Weeks Ago

On the day Mydei signed the contract, it felt like the hours were simultaneously fleeting and unending.

The hours were fleeting because, in hindsight, he could hardly recall the details of what went down during the morning and the afternoon. All he remembered was the comprehensive meeting that transpired between him and his manager, and the Flame-Chasers themselves and their own manager. Both parties had met and finalized the details of what their contracts would entail, and by the time Mydei had signed the pages, he was ready to celebrate his win with a solitary unwinding in his own room.

However, he was immediately pulled into the celebratory party the Flame-Chasers were hosting that evening, and that was when the hours turned from surprisingly brief to excruciatingly endless.

The club Mydei was in now was a little smaller than others he had gone to in the past, and tonight’s event was strictly accessible by invitation only. He would have thought that the combination of the limited space and the limited crowd would make the whole ordeal less overstimulating for him, but all that did was make the venue appear more packed than it already was. Despite its walls made of black marble, its tables made of dark slates, and its couches and chairs made of smooth velvet, the stylish interior was a mere background to the way everyone was losing themselves to the alcohol, to the music, to the conversations. Mydei was not a fan of extroverted spaces to begin with; being in one, no matter how luxurious it was, was already testing his limits.

But even though Mydei found himself doubting the enjoyability of such an occasion, he knew he had to stay, at least for a few more hours. Apart from being the opening act for the Flame-Chasers, he was here to further broaden his horizons. This party, which tided in not only the band members but their sponsors and close affiliates as well, was a chance to promote Mydei’s name even further.

After all, the only reason Mydei was presented with this opportunity in the first place was because one of his solo performances had gone viral on the Internet. Overnight, he went from being just another indie singer to someone worth keeping an eye on. His record label could hardly keep up with inquiries regarding his availability, and they had to filter out multiple invitations before finally settling on the Flame-Chasers’ proposal.

Despite his introverted nature, Mydei knew he needed to maximize this momentum and ensure that he wasn’t just a passing name in the music industry.

That didn’t mean he didn’t get tired, though. In fact, he was frankly more exhausted than he’d ever been so far.

“Enjoying yourself?”

Mydei didn’t even know he was staring into space until the familiar voice brought him out of his reverie. Beside him, the lead singer of the Flame-Chasers himself, Phainon, settled into the available space beside Mydei.

Mydei took in the sight of him. In most of his public appearances, Phainon was notable for wearing two things: a dark choker that opened to the side to reveal the tattoo of a sun on his neck, and a white leather jacket studded with spikes at the sleeves and held together by a belt at the hem. He wore both of these things now, alongside a pair of fitted jeans and a pair of low boots.

Mydei, not one to be underdressed, was in a similar get-up. He had opted to wear the usual black leather jacket he wore during his solo performances. Leather bracelets adorned his wrists, and his waist was dripping with several silver chains. A pair of leather pants dressed his legs, accentuated by the boots that came up to the midpoint of his shins.

Outwardly, Mydei fitted right in. But to say that he was enjoying himself seemed like a stretch.

He offered Phainon a small shrug in response. Though the music wasn’t loud, he still had to raise his voice to be heard over the chatter of the place.

“It could be worse.”

Phainon smiled knowingly. “You don’t have to pretend. My first party within the A-lister scene was overwhelming for me too.” He had a glass in one hand, which he tipped to his lips before placing it against the table before them. He gestured to the empty space in front of Mydei. “You don’t drink?”

Mydei shook his head. “I like to take care of my voice.”

“It’s not so bad,” Phainon countered. “I still drink too, just moderately. It takes the edge off of things.”

Mydei forced himself to recline against the couch. He was sitting too stiffly anyway. “Does that mean you still get nervous before shows and tours?”

“Of course. I don’t think that ever fully goes away.” Phainon draped his arms against the back of the couch and glanced at Mydei. “Why? Are you nervous?”

“A little,” Mydei confessed.

“Ha! Then you’re already better than me.” Phainon stared at the small crowd, his gaze looking but not quite seeing, as he replayed a memory only he could see. “I was a mess before our first big tour. My bandmates, Cas and Anaxa, were lucky; they could afford to drown their restlessness with alcohol. Drinking moderately is fine, but not if it’s days before a big event. I had to find other means to deal with the anxiety.”

“Such as?” Mydei inquired. Perhaps he could learn a thing or two from Phainon in this regard.

“Ah, well,” Phainon merely said, sipping his drink. “They’re the physical kind.”

It was Mydei’s turn to blush. Phainon need not say anything more. “Oh.”

Neither of them looked at the other for a while as Phainon set his glass back down against the table.

Shit, Mydei thought. He shouldn’t have asked.

Mydei almost sighed in relief. He was glad for Phainon’s quick recovery. “What do you mean?”

“Cas usually asks for a certain brand of liquor to bring with her on tour, so I make sure our manager procures that for her beforehand.” Phainon smiled. “So if you have any special requests, feel free to name them.”

“Oh.” Phainon tilted his head. This time, he held Mydei’s gaze, and it was Mydei who couldn’t afford to hold his.

Phainon, who looked every bit like a scolded puppy, brightened upon seeing Mydei. He cupped his hands over his mouth, his lips parting as he wished him well.

“Break a leg, Mydei!” he cheered. Then his smile softened into one of complete sincerity. “You’ll do great.”

Mydei swallowed. Given how fast they were moving, there was nothing left to do but nod back at him. Then he turned away from Phainon, his attention shifting from him to Aglaea completely. “I—”

“We’ll talk about it later,” she cut in immediately. She glanced at him. “For now, you need to get your head in your performance. I trust that you are prepared enough for your set?”

Mydei decided to drop the subject. She was right anyway. The concert superseded whatever foolishness she caught them in. “I am.”

“Perfect. Because we have wasted enough time.”

Before he knew it, Mydei was being shepherded into another room, a wide rectangular waiting area filled with equipment and wires. There was nothing drab and gray about this one, unlike the corridor which they’d come from. Instead, a group of technicians ran about the place, all of them boasting earpieces or walkie-talkies of their own, each of them deep into conversation with someone else on the line.

But Mydei had no time to fully take in the scene. He allowed himself to be led by Aglaea and the crew instead, multiple people surrounding him all at once to brush up on his make-up or straighten his clothes or hand him his crimson red electric guitar. Then they fitted him with an earpiece of his own, explained that his guitar was already tuned and ready, and instructed him to align himself with the micstand already prepared upon the stage.

At any other time, Mydei would have already been overwhelmed. This was a calibre of a production unlike everything he has known, and he would have easily gone under from the pressure of everyone’s expectations.

But Phainon was right about one thing. Whatever they shared in the janitor’s closet was nothing more than offer to ease his mind.

And ease it did.

Mydei was asked to stand over a circular platform, and another technician explained that it would rise in about ten minutes to take him up to center stage. Mydei nodded in acknowledgement, and then the crew began to dissipate, each of them trickling away to make preparations of their own now that Mydei was all ready to go.

Aglaea, who had taken a step back to let everyone fuss over him, finally stepped forward once more. She beheld Mydei, her emotions carefully hidden from her face.

“Are you ready?” she asked. If Mydei didn’t know better, he would have thought that she sounded almost gentle.

Mydei’s fingers tightened against the neck of his guitar as he adjusted the strap over his shoulder. “I am,” he said. Then, when Aglaea continued to stare at him, he repeated it in a more confident tone. “I’m ready.”

Aglaea finally nodded. Then, at last, she smiled. “Think of it as any other performance you’ve had in the past.”

“Hmm,” Mydei mused. “I don’t think I’ve ever had fifteen thousand pairs of eyes on me before.”

Aglaea snorted. Then, in unison, both her earpiece and Mydei’s crackled with static. A voice advised them that Mydei was set to go up on stage, and Aglaea stepped back and away from the platform.

“You’ll do great,” Aglaea whispered, repeating Phainon’s well wishes onto Mydei.

Mydei nodded. “Thank you,” he replied just as softly.

Then, in no time at all and with someone counting down into his ear, Mydei felt the platform beneath him begin to rise.

Mydei took a deep breath. The interior of the waiting room fell away, plunging him into momentary darkness. Above him, he heard the excited screams of the crowd, their muffled cries turning sharper and sharper the closer he got to the stage. Mydei reached up to adjust his earpiece, pressing it deeper into his ear so that he wouldn’t miss any cue he may be given.

And then he was on stage, his eyes taking in the complete darkness of the stadium, illuminated only by the scattering of flashlights shining from cameras and phones. Mydei’s fingers clenched around his guitar, his one last purchase to hold on to solid ground, his one last reminder that this was it, this was happening, this was real.

The platform stopped rising, finally clicking into place against the floor of the stage. Mydei heard the sound of drumsticks coming together, counting down from three.

Think of it as any other performance you’ve had in the past, Aglaea had advised.

Two.

Mydei grabbed the the micstand and pulled it closer to him. Even in the dimness, he could see its silhouette positioned perfectly before him.

One.

Sorry, Aglaea, Mydei thought. I can’t.

Then the spotlight was upon him, and Mydei ran his hand over the strings of his guitar, surrendering himself to the music as he summoned the first note of the first song to his very first tour performance.

Because this is so much better than anything I’ve ever known.

Before him, the crowd responded in kind. Their shouts reverberated throughout the place, almost loud enough to drown out his own song blaring from the speakers.

Mydei lifted his head and stared back at them. He took in the thousands before him, all screaming and all chanting his name, over and over and over.

Then he smiled. And, leaving behind every trace of his anxieties far below him, Mydei stepped up to the mic and began to sing.

It was a feeling unlike everything he had ever known. Mydei knew that he was the one strumming the chords on his own guitar, playing one of the very first songs he had ever written and released. Mydei knew that he was the one singing over the microphone, his voice loud and clear as he sang the lyrics with perfect pitch and timing. Mydei knew that he was the one performing, his head bobbing as he let the band behind him back up his tunes and his vocals.

But, at the same time, he felt like he was watching everything unfold from outside of his own body. It felt like he was another bystander on the mosh pit, staring up at him in wonder as the gleam of the stones on his leather jacket caught the light and reflected it back to them. It felt like he was another person on the seats, screaming his name as they recorded Mydei playing a riff over his guitar, fingers steady and sure as they coaxed the music out of the instrument. It felt like he was another person on the sidelines, gleeful tears welling in their eyes as they watched Mydei play song after song after song as the opening act for the Flame-Chasers.

It was intoxicating and overwhelming and completely out of this world.

And Mydei couldn’t get enough of it.

Whatever worries he had previously been preoccupied with seemed so distant now, like they were so far past behind him they were almost nonexistent. Before he knew it, he had finished the whole of his line-up, and his next and final cue was being whispered to him in the small speaker of his earpiece.

“Get ready,” the voice said. “Entering the Flame-Chasers in five minutes.”

Mydei continued to play, finishing the last chorus of his own song. Still, he moved discreetly across the stage, stepping up to his next blocking as he made space for the main act that was set to enter.

Then, once he was in position, he strummed the last of his song and let the sound hang in the air as he concluded his own individual setlist.

With heaving shoulders, he stared up at the crowd, drinking in all their praise and all their approval and all their showered glory.

“Thank you all for tonight,” Mydei said into the mic. He gave the crowd time to yell back their love, grinning up at them as he basked in the afterglow of his performance.

“However,” Mydei started, once he felt a slight lull in their cheers, “I do have one last song to play for you all. It’s a cover of a popular track most of you are probably familiar with. But here’s the catch.”

Slowly, the lights began to flicker shut. One by one, portions of the stage fell into darkness: first the backmost portion, then the left side, then the right. The whole stadium turned dark until only Mydei’s spot was bathed in light.

He grabbed the mic and pressed his lips against it. “This time, I’m not singing alone.”

And then the light over him went dark.

Mydei knew what was happening now. After all, this was something he and the Flame-Chasers had planned and arranged right from the start. Despite the totality of darkness, he knew that Castorice and Anaxa were now rushing over to their instruments, trading places with Mydei’s own team as they did so.

And as faux smoke began to fill the floor of the stage, as Mydei began to play the first few chords of the song they were covering, as the stadium became a cage of everyone’s excitement, Mydei knew that Phainon was beginning to rise from the platform on which he had been previously standing upon.

“Alright, alright,” Phainon’s familiar voice began to blare from the speakers. Beside Mydei, the platform rose higher and higher until he could see the silhouette of the white-haired singer appear.

“Alright, alright,” Mydei sang back.

And when the platform locked into place, when Castorice slammed her drumsticks against her drums, when Anaxa began to strum across his bass guitar, that was when the lights all came back on. It illuminated the stage in full, revealing the Flame-Chasers now positioned over the stage, with Mydei standing alongside Phainon.

“Alright, alright! It’s a hell of a feeling though! It’s a hell of a feeling though!” Phainon leaned into his mic, raising his arms out. “Sing it with us!”

Mydei continued to sing through the familiarity of the song, even as the crowd began to yell the lyrics back at them. Phainon, meanwhile, had the widest beam on his face as he pointed his own microphone back at the audience. Beneath the spotlight, he looked like the sun, blazing in a glory of white and gold, as he gathered the crowd to sing with them.

As soon as the refrain ended, he took back his mic and placed it back against his lips. With one glance and a wink towards Mydei, he slid right into the verse, continuing to sing alongside him without missing a beat.

Ah, Mydei thought distantly, even as he continued to perform. So this is what a seasoned rockstar looks like.

And though they had rehearsed this multiple times before, Mydei found himself falling down into a different kind of feeling altogether.

None of the rehearsals they had, he realized, could compare to the real thing.

Mydei allowed himself to be possessed by the music, his body and soul completely at the mercy of the song he and the Flame-Chasers were sharing. He allowed the notes to lead him by the hand, to take him into a different kind of excitement unlike anything he has ever known. He even allowed Phainon to guide him, both of them moving around one another like they were the sun and moon orbiting over the other.

And if he had been just a little more conscious, Mydei could have avoided what came next. If he had been just a little less passionate, he could have anticipated what was to come.

If he had been just a little less greedy and ambitious, he could have changed the trajectory of his life and prevented the mess he was about to plunge himself into.

But Mydei was too caught up in the moment to notice the ropes of wires by his feet. By the time he did notice it, the toe of his boot was already entangled upon them, ensnaring him and bringing him down to their clutches.

And before he knew it, before he understood what was happening, before he could even begin to process why his line of sight was suddenly askew, he was falling, falling, falling.

Only then did he realize what was going on, and he braced an arm out, already ready to break his fall.

Shit.

Except, instead of solid ground, he found himself resting against solid warmth instead. Then he was staring face to face at a pair of familiar blue, so bright and concerned and just as surprised as Mydei was.

“When I told you to break a leg,” Phainon said, voice breathless from singing and voice strained from catching Mydei’s body weight, “I didn’t mean it quite literally.”

Mydei was keenly aware of three things, all at once. Firstly, he was suddenly all too aware of how close they were. Phainon was leaning over, his knees and his waist bent as he positioned himself to brace Mydei’s fall and hold him up. Their legs were tangled together and their faces were near enough that Phainon’s expression was almost blurring in Mydei’s eyes. Drops of sweat from Phainon’s bangs fell across Mydei, and every drop that fell rolled down the bridge of his nose.

Secondly, he was all too aware of how tightly they were holding onto one another. The arm that was holding Mydei was the same one that was holding his microphone, and Mydei could feel the equipment digging over his lower back now. Mydei, who previously had his own mic in his hand, had dropped it on the stage completely. Instead, both his hands were clutching the collars of Phainon’s white jacket, fingers tight as he clung onto him for dear life.

And lastly, he was all too aware of everyone around them gasping. Then those gasps rose in pitch and in volume, rising higher and higher until it was a cacophony of shrieks that broke whatever bubble he and Phainon shared.

Mydei whirled around, his eyes wide as he beheld the packed stadium. From this angle, each and every one of the spotlights shone directly onto his line of sight. Still, he could see through them enough to know that all eyes were on him and the main vocalist of the Flame-Chasers.

Not only that, but every phone, every camera, every video recording device was now held up high to capture the scene they were putting onstage.

Oh no, Mydei thought. He turned back to Phainon, who was still looking down at him with an unreadable expression. His eyes were imploring him to know something, to realize one thing, to understand a message he was trying to convey. But all Mydei could glean from it were his words from nights and nights past.

The last thing either of us needs is a rumor amidst everything going on.

Mydei felt his fingers tighten against Phainon, hoping he could quietly convey his apology in that manner.

Whatever rumors were going to come out of this—and he knew there would be an abundance of them—he really hoped they would be kind to him and Phainon.

Because he knew that, as of this moment, he was in deep fucking shit.

During their first year of fame, right after they garnered the people’s attention with their band’s debut single, the Flame-Chasers began to receive a steady string of offers from various brands. From the bigger, luxurious ones to the smaller, rising ones, each and every one of those names sought for their partnership and collaboration to boost their products.

Phainon remembered his first shoot clearly. After all, he had been nothing short of ecstatic but nervous on the day itself. He’d been rolling around a lollipop in his mouth the whole morning, a habit he once had to help him manage more nerve-wracking situations.

“Do you think they’d kick me out if I did something extremely stupid on set?” he’d asked. Back then, all they had was a van that carried them to and from places, nothing as grand as the tour bus they had now, and he and his bandmates were all seated at the back.

Cyrene, who had occupied the passenger seat and was busy arranging their schedules, had looked up from her tablet. When she’d looked over her shoulder at him, her pink bob had moved with her. “Are you planning something?”

Anaxa, who had been quiet up until that point, had sighed. “Not entirely out of the realm of possibility.”

“I’m not planning anything!” Phainon had protested. Then, realizing the question he’d posed sounded misleading, he’d clarified, “What if I accidentally ruined one of their leather products? Or break one of their bag straps? You know, honest mistakes like that.”

“Phainon,” Castorice had said, horror etched onto her face, “I really, really hope you don’t break any of the things they’re asking us to model. And please don’t attract such negative thoughts.”

Phainon had left it at that. Castorice had a point anyway; there was no use thinking of such possibilities when he could work to avoid those mishaps instead.

And Phainon had succeeded for the most part. He had broken none of the things they were modeling.

The only thing he did manage to break was a lightstand. He had accidentally leaned too far against it while waiting for his turn to pose, and he had been unable to break its fall in his panic. It had fallen and shattered into a hundred shards of glass on the floor, and they’d had to stop the shoot for an hour or so until they had everything cleaned up. Phainon had been too ashamed to face the heads of the brand after that, and he’d kept his head bowed as he issued apology after apology to them.

While they did assure him that things were alright, the rumor that Phainon was a clumsy rookie of a star circulated behind the scenes for a long, long time. It had taken him multiple projects to regain the trust of crewmen again, and even then, they still took extra caution to always position him away from fragile items from then on.

But the rumor had passed and Phainon had cleared his name and now he was someone the brands invited back time and time again.

That was a lesson he learned during the first year of his career. Whatever rumor went around could always be undone, given the right amount of time and the right amount of effort and, if needed, the right amount of connections.

He just didn’t know if Mydei knew that yet.

Or, scratch that. He knew for certain that Mydei didn’t know that yet.

That fragment of a memory ricocheted in his mind now as he sat at the breakfast table of their hotel lobby. It was the morning after the first concert of their tour, and the plan had been for Phainon’s and Mydei’s teams to eat a hearty meal together in the private function room before they made their way to their next tour stop. It was meant to be a celebratory breakfast of sorts, an acknowledgement that they had gotten past the first show.

Instead, a solemn atmosphere loomed over the table where Phainon, Anaxa, and Castorice sat. Mydei, Aglaea, and Cyrene were still nowhere in sight, though their manager assured them that they were already coming down from their rooms.

“So,” Castorice started, her eyes flitting away from her phone briefly to address her bandmate. “It seems like you and Mydei are still trending.”

Phainon, who was busy scrolling through his own phone, raised his brows. “I’m well aware.”

And it was true. After their show had concluded, the first thing he did once he was alone was throw himself down a rabbit hole of all the things people were saying about their concert. He didn’t even need to search his or Mydei’s name; the posts were already curated and arranged on his timeline the moment he opened his app.

The posts went on and on, not just from what he could see in Twitter, but in the other social media platforms as well. It was all he saw anywhere he went, the videos all boasting various angles of the moment Mydei had tripped on stage and the exact time Phainon had whirled to catch him.

Not like Phainon needed any of those to remind him of what happened. Even without the thousands of video recordings circulating online, Phainon had that memory memorized. He recalled, with perfect clarity, the moment he noticed Mydei walking towards the tangled rope wires of their instruments. He recalled, with flawless precision, the moment Phainon stepped closer to him, his arms still hesitant on what he would do with his microphone and his own guitar.

Then he recalled, with absolute remembrance, the moment Phainon had caught him, his blue eyes locking with Mydei’s gold ones as he quietly asked him with his stare, Are you alright?

He was still waiting for Mydei’s answer to that question.

Phainon placed his phone on the table now and sighed. “Don’t you think you guys are blowing this out of proportion?” he said. “Bad publicity is still publicity.”

“So you admit,” Anaxa remarked, “that this is bad?”

“Uhm. Well.” Phainon scratched the back of his head. “For our managers, I guess this is a PR nightmare. But if they play our cards right–which they will–it can be something we use to our advantage. It’s not like something truly awful happened.”

Anaxa crossed his arms over his chest. “That may be,” he agreed. “But you already know that romantic rumors are some of the worst kinds. The press will begin to hound us like never before, and we’ll have to tighten our security to avoid our privacies from being invaded by them.”

“Okay, point taken.” Phainon threaded his fingers together and rested his chin atop of them. “But don’t act like it’s Mydei’s fault. It’s not like he tripped himself on purpose. We made mistakes when we were rookies too.”

“You’re right. It’s not his fault.” Anaxa narrowed his eyes. “It’s yours for catching him in such an intimate manner.”

“My fault?” Phainon asked incredulously. “So was I supposed to just let him fall?”

“No, but you didn’t even have to hold him for that long. You could have just righted him back up instead of keeping him in your arms. Would you have caught me in the same manner if I was the one who fell?”

“I wouldn’t have caught you at all because you’re being obtuse about this.”

Before Anaxa could get another word in, Phainon heard the amused chuckle of someone behind him.

“Pointing fingers over spilled milk will do us no good,” the sweet and familiar voice of his manager intoned. “Instead, why don’t we try working out a solution that benefits all of us?”

Phainon turned, the legs of his seat scraping against the floor as he moved. Standing a few feet away from him, just by the open door, were the remaining three people their group had been missing.

Cyrene entered the room first, her posture poised and her expression calm as always. There was no doubt that she had been up all night assessing the situation, but whatever stress may be plaguing her did not reflect in the way she carried herself. If anything, her smile remained composed and bright.

Half a step behind her was Aglaea. Whereas Cyrene was the personification of being carefree, Aglaea looked a little more stern. From her face alone, it was difficult to tell just how disapproving she was of the predicament they were now all in. The only consolation Phainon had was that she looked like she had come to an agreement with Cyrene, evident in the way she looked to her for confirmation and support.

And, behind the two women, was the person Phainon had been waiting to see all this time. Although there were dark circles beneath his eyes, evidence of a night poorly spent tossing and turning, he looked far less avoidant than he had been hours ago. In fact, he looked at everyone in the room head-on, as if he had come to terms with the mistake he’d made and was ready to discuss what became of it next. When his eyes finally landed on Phainon, Phainon felt the tense set of his own shoulders relax.

Mydei.

Mydei, to his credit, gave him a slight nod before he looked away once more.

Phainon continued to watch him as Mydei took the empty seat beside him. Cyrene helped herself to the chair beside Castorice, and Aglaea took her place beside Mydei. Now, with the whole team complete and settled, Cyrene placed her tablet before her, clasped her hands together, and gave everyone a reassuring smile.

“Let’s cut to the chase,” she started. Even though it was still the start of the day, she was already dressed and styled pristinely, ever the image of calmness. “I understand that this is a very interesting turn of events. But it’s nothing we can’t control, and it’s nothing I haven’t heard of before.”

Cyrene casted her gaze upon Mydei, and her smile softened. “So please. Don’t feel too bad about it. After all, handling this is part of our job description, both Aglaea and I.”

Mydei nodded. Still, he didn’t say a word.

“The most important part is that Mydei is unscathed,” she went on. “That would have been a far more difficult dilemma for us to solve if we had to suddenly pull out our opening act for the rest of the tour.”

“Are we supposed to let the rumors die down then?” Castorice piqued. She tapped several times over her phone before revealing her screen to everyone on the table. “They already have fancams of what happened.”

Phainon watched the video playing from her device, the corners of his lips twitching amusedly as he beheld the way the video cut and transitioned to various angles of Mydei’s fall and Phainon’s rescue. Beside him, Mydei sighed and rubbed at his temples, clearly embarrassed to review the spectacle.

Cyrene, to her credit, watched the entirety of the video with rapt attention.

“Cute,” she remarked with a laugh, once the video looped around back to the beginning. “But going back to Castorice’s question, the answer is no.”

Castorice blinked. She pulled her phone back to herself and exited from the app, plunging the room back into quiet. “No?”

Cyrene shook her head. When she looked at Phainon and Mydei next, her resolve was absolute. “This time, I want you to feed into the rumors.”

And, just like that, there was silence. Complete and utter silence. If Phainon didn’t know any better, he would have thought that a vacuum of gravity and space had come and swallowed their group whole. Everyone, save for Aglaea, was too busy staring at Cyrene in shock. Even Phainon had traded his usual cheery demeanor for one of complete dismay.

What? he thought to himself. Feed into the rumors? What game was Cyrene playing at this time? Was he just mishearing things?

“Wait,” he finally said. He leaned forward, his movements slow and hesitant, as he struggled to comprehend her suggestion. “You want us to what now?”

Cyrene remained unfazed. All she did was reach for her tablet, angling it so that everyone could see the charts and sheets of numbers she pulled up on its screen. “Aglaea and I have been monitoring the public reception and the tour sales overnight.”

She swiped over the numbers, and though Phainon understood little of the data being presented, he understood enough of the line graph and its rising green arrow.

“It seems like Cas was right,” Cyrene went on. “The two of you have become very popular among the fans, and everyone wants to see more.”

“The shows that were yet to sell out all sold out last night,” Aglaea added. She gestured to Cyrene’s tablet as the pink-haired manager continued to flash them another tally of numbers. “Even now, we have been receiving numerous requests to add additional stops to the tour, all for a chance to see you.”

Beside him, Phainon heard Mydei inhale a sharp breath. Then, for the first time this morning, he spoke. “I’m not sure I follow.”

Phainon glanced at him. With how deep his frown was, Mydei was definitely following the conversation. But, like Phainon, he was in complete disbelief at the solution their managers were presenting to them.

“The chemistry you and Phainon displayed on stage was rather captivating,” Cyrene said. “Given that you are both already, well, close with one another–”

Phainon and Mydei both coughed at the same time, their thoughts converging to the moment Aglaea caught them red handed yesterday.

“–it shouldn’t be too hard to fan the flames here and there,” Cyrene finished.

“Having the both of you as the face of this tour can also put Anaxa and Castorice a little less out of the spotlight,” Aglaea said. “Something I heard Anaxa express concerns over.”

Across from them, Anaxa hummed. “It sounds plausible in theory. But we will be followed by the paparazzi just as much as you are.”

“Not as closely as Phainon and Mydei will be.”

Phainon drummed his fingers across the table. “So that’s the play this time? Mydei and I will be the sacrificial lamb to take the brunt of the press?”

Cyrene pouted. “Please don’t word it so poorly,” she said. “Of everyone in this table, you are the most used to the attention from the press anyway. Mydei just has to learn a trick or two from you on how to play pretend.”

“And what are we doing this for exactly?” Mydei asked.

“Profit,” Aglaea replied simply. “The revenue from the sold tickets have already exceeded our expectations, but they continue to rise in number. Moreover, the brand deals and partnerships after last night’s stunt have already begun to pour in. Apart from financial profit, these additional projects will mean more exposure and opportunities down the line.”

Mydei leaned back against his seat. It was difficult for Phainon to glean whether or not he approved of this proposal. “What happens if the people find out that this is all for show? Wouldn’t that backfire on us?”

Cyrene shook her head. “We’re not asking you to be explicit about the status of your relationship. In fact, I would encourage you to keep it as subtle as possible. When asked in interviews, you are even free to acknowledge that there is truly nothing between you.” She flashed them a saccharine smile. “After all, the best lies are the ones with a hint of truth in them.”

Aglaea nodded in agreement. “All we are asking is that you string the people along, just a little bit,” she said. “Just enough to keep their attention on us.”

“If we refuse this,” Mydei asked, “what happens then?”

Cyrene opened her mouth, already ready to give him an objective reply. But Phainon turned to Mydei and beat her to the punchline, answering in her stead.

“If we were to actively stamp down the people’s perceptions of us, it would only be a fight we’d lose,” he said, catching on to Cyrene’s reason. Mydei glanced at him, and Phainon forced himself to keep their shared eye contact. “Regardless of what we say at this point, they will continue to think that the two of us are dating anyway. We might as well run with the narratives in their heads and maximize profit while we’re at it.”

From across the table, Cyrene hummed in approval. “It’s exactly as Phainon said.”

Mydei rubbed a hand over his lips. “I’m assuming I have little say on this matter.”

“Well, I am open to ideas!” Cyrene amended. “If you have a better suggestion on how to go about this, then be my guest.” She nodded at Phainon. “Same goes for you.”

Phainon pressed his hands against his lips, his mind churning with a thousand thoughts and possibilities per minute. “We only have to pretend until the end of the tour, right?”

“Correct.”

Phainon sighed. No matter which way he looked at it, Cyrene’s solution was the most feasible at the moment. The people were going to keep talking anyway. They might as well take advantage of the momentum already preceding them.

They all let the last note linger in the air, and Phainon continued to let his outstretched arm hover in the space between him and Mydei. It almost felt like time had stopped, suspending all of them into a picture of yearning, a still frame of what it meant to embody the song into reality.

Then Phainon took a deep, deep breath, and he let his arm fall back to his side, and the moment shattered.

“Alright,” Anaxa said, speaking up first. He set his bass guitar down in its stand before resting his hands on his knees. “Are we all done now?”

Phainon turned to him.

“Yeah, we’re done,” Mydei answered first. He slung his guitar over his head and placed it in its own stand. He took the hem of his shirt and lifted it up, exposing the muscles of his abs as he wiped the sweat from his cheeks. “We have to get changed anyway.”

Phainon took another deep breath. Then he set his own guitar down and gave a slow clap. “Good job, everyone!” he cheered. “That was a perfect run!”

The four of them began to exit the stage, every one of them already resigned to return backstage. Phainon was the last to linger, falling five steps behind everyone else. When he looked up, he was pleasantly surprised to find Mydei falling back, looking at him as he waited for Phainon to catch up.

“Yes?” Phainon said, batting his lashes at him. “Were you waiting for me?”

Mydei scowled. Once Phainon reached him, they began to walk side by side. “Already getting on my nerves.”

Phainon laughed. Then, after another moment’s hesitation, he grabbed Mydei’s arm and hugged it tight. “I’m sorry,” he murmured against his bicep.

“Get off of me,” Mydei said, shrugging him off. “You’re not slick.”

“What are you implying?” Phainon said, holding onto him tighter and pressing his cheek against Mydei’s muscles. “I’m just a man begging for forgiveness!”

“And what,” Mydei began, “are you apologizing for?”

Phainon stopped. He glanced up at Mydei.

For saying you’re just someone I sleep with, he thought, and that you’re nothing more than that. Even if it’s the truth.

Because it is the truth.

Right?

“For being an idiot,” he said at last. When he smiled again, it was a little tight at the edges. “For hurting your feelings.”

Mydei sighed. He reached over with his other arm and flicked the top of Phainon’s head. “You didn’t hurt my feelings.”

“Liar,” Phainon accused.

“Maybe,” Mydei agreed. When he pushed Phainon off of him this time, it was gentle but absolute. Phainon allowed himself to be directed away. “Let’s just put it behind us so we can perform without any hitches.”

Phainon straightened. As he did, the back of his hand brushed against Mydei’s.

“Whatever you say,” he said, as they continued walking backstage towards their dressing room. He glanced at Mydei. “Like I said, though, I don’t make the same mistakes twice.”

Mydei merely shrugged. “We’ll see.”

Phainon smiled. We’ll see indeed, he thought to himself. After all, only time will tell whether he could prove his words true this time.
